canonicalEditorial.summary: On April 17, 1966, Bill Russell was named player-coach of the Boston Celtics, becoming the first Black head coach in the history of a major U.S. professional sports league. He won two more championships as player-coach (1968, 1969), on top of the eight he won as a player. He was inducted into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame as a player in 1975 and as a coach in 2021.
canonicalEditorial.historicalContext: Russell's coaching and playing careers were both spent with the Boston Celtics; the Hall of Fame in Springfield, MA is the most concrete surviving site tied to both of his enshrinements.

entities.displayName: Autherine Lucy's Enrollment at the University of Alabama

canonicalEditorial.summary: Autherine Lucy became the University of Alabama's first Black student on February 3, 1956, but after mobs rioted against her for three days, the university suspended and then expelled her, a wrong it did not formally reverse until 1988, allowing her to complete her degree in 1992.
canonicalEditorial.historicalContext: The University of Alabama's 1956 mob violence against Lucy remains, by scholarly consensus, the most violent anti-integration response to any post-Brown v. Board college desegregation, foreshadowing the federal confrontation that would return to the same campus in 1963.

canonicalBasis.note: Readmitted in 1988, when the university's board voted to lift her expulsion; she returned to complete her degree, graduating in 1992 alongside her daughter.
Enrolled on February 3, 1956, becoming the first African American student at the University of Alabama, before mobs chased and attacked her over the following days.

released.summary: Autherine Lucy's enrollment at the University of Alabama was the first attempt to integrate the institution. In 1956, she enrolled as a graduate student in library sciences after securing a court order against racial exclusion. Violent protests followed, and the university suspended and later expelled her within days, citing its inability to provide a safe learning environment. Her enrollment struggle became a test case after the Supreme Court's 1955 Brown v. Board of Education decision outlawed segregation.
released.historicalContext: The University of Alabama did not integrate until Vivian Malone and James Hood registered for classes in 1963. Lucy's expulsion was rescinded in 1980, and she returned to earn a master's degree in 1992.

canonicalEditorial.summary: The Golden Thirteen were the first African American commissioned and warrant officers in the U.S. Navy, trained in 1944 amid WWII-era civil rights pressures. Despite systemic barriers, they overcame accelerated training and institutional skepticism to become officers, though only 13 of 16 graduates received commissions.
canonicalEditorial.historicalContext: The Golden Thirteen emerged during WWII as part of broader civil rights efforts to integrate the U.S. military. Their commissioning followed President Roosevelt’s 1941 Executive Order 8802 banning racial discrimination in defense industries, and preceded Truman’s 1948 desegregation of the armed forces. Their success challenged segregationist policies that had confined Black sailors to menial roles since 1919.

canonicalBasis.note: Trained at Great Lakes Naval Training Station.

canonicalEditorial.summary: Denied flight training in the United States because of her race and sex, Bessie Coleman traveled to France and, on June 15, 1921, earned an international pilot's license from the Fédération Aéronautique Internationale, becoming the first Black woman and first Black American to hold a pilot's license. She toured the U.S. as a barnstorming exhibition flier until her death in 1926.
canonicalEditorial.historicalContext: Coleman studied French and self-funded travel to France for flight school since no American school would train a Black woman. She dreamed of opening a flight school for Black aviators but died in a 1926 exhibition-flight accident in Jacksonville, Florida before realizing it; her Chicago grave remains the most visited site tied to her legacy.

canonicalBasis.note: Buried at Lincoln Cemetery in Alsip, Illinois, where Black aviators continue a tradition of dropping flowers during flyovers of her grave each year.

canonicalEditorial.summary: David Blackwell, a statistician who earned his PhD at age 22 from the University of Illinois, became UC Berkeley's first Black tenured professor in 1954 and, in 1965, the first African American elected to the National Academy of Sciences. He co-developed the Rao-Blackwell theorem and mentored more than 60 doctoral students.
canonicalEditorial.historicalContext: Before Berkeley, Blackwell was repeatedly denied faculty positions at predominantly white universities and taught at Southern University, Clark College, and Howard University, where he chaired the math department; UC Berkeley named a residence hall for him in 2018.

canonicalBasis.note: Chaired UC Berkeley's statistics department from 1957 to 1961 and co-developed the Rao-Blackwell theorem, a foundational result in statistical estimation theory.

draft.summary: Autherine Lucy's enrollment at the University of Alabama was the first attempt to integrate the institution. In 1956, she enrolled as a graduate student in library sciences after securing a court order against racial exclusion. Violent protests followed, and the university suspended and later expelled her within days, citing its inability to provide a safe learning environment. Her enrollment struggle became a test case after the Supreme Court's 1955 Brown v. Board of Education decision outlawed segregation.

summaryCitations.quote: The first attempt to integrate the university occurred in 1956 when Autherine Lucy successfully enrolled on February 3 as a graduate student in library sciences after she secured a court order preventing the university from rejecting her application on the basis of race.

In the face of violent protests against her attendance, Lucy was suspended (and later outright expelled) three days later by the board of trustees on the basis of being unable to provide a safe learning environment for her.

In 1955, the Brown vs. Board of Education decision outlawing segregation came down from the U.S. Supreme Court, and it became clear to Shores and the NAACP that the Myers/Lucy case would be the first test.

draft.historicalContext: The University of Alabama did not integrate until Vivian Malone and James Hood registered for classes in 1963. Lucy's expulsion was rescinded in 1980, and she returned to earn a master's degree in 1992.

historicalContextCitations.quote: The university was not integrated until 1963 when Vivian Malone and James Hood registered for classes on June 11.
